title: A Tale of Blood and Ashes: The Exeter Vampires | Halloween Season
description_html:
In 1800s America, something terrifying is feeding on the quiet town of Exeter. As members of George Brown's family succumb one by one, the town considers drastic measures to protect the living from the dead.

For a list of sources, see the show notes at timharford.com

Cautionary Tales is celebrating Halloween with a full month of paranormal themed episodes. If you have a spooky story or a skeptical question, get in touch at tales@pushkin.fm. cues.t: Pushkin. In the town of Griswold, Connecticut, some children are playing on an old gravel mine.
It's spring 1990.
Years of excavation have carved this place into a series of steep, grey banks.
Abandoned now, it's become the neighbourhood toboggan run.
The children scramble up the slopes, boots sliding over loose stones, and then careen toward the quarry floor, shrieking with laughter.
Small rocks skitter after them.
Then, on one run, the earth gives up something larger than the average pebble, something smooth and brown.
It tumbles through the air and rolls to a stop at the bottom.
The children form a curious circle around the object.
It stares blindly up at them.
Two hollow sockets.
A sunken nose.
A gaping jaw packed tight with dirt.
Their laughter fades.
This isn't a rock.
Soon, yellow crime scene tape cordons off this playground.
In the 1980s, a serial killer terrorised Connecticut... murdering at least eight women and girls.
The police think that the children might have uncovered another of his victims.
It's quickly apparent, however, that this skull is from another century.
The state archaeologist, Nick Bellantoni, is called in, and the investigation now shifts from crime scene to historical dig.
Bellantoni and his team set to work shaving away the soil, first with flat-edged shovels, Then, with delicate brushes and bamboo picks, coffin after coffin emerges from the hillside.
Some of the skeletons inside bear the marks of violent injury.
Others still have tufts of hair clinging to their skulls.
In one corner, seven much smaller skeletons lie clustered together.
Children. This isn't just a gravel pit.
It's an unmarked cemetery.
One grave stands apart, a stone crypt poking through the mine face.
Bellantoni labels it burial plot number four.
He begins lifting away the flat, heavy stones that form the crypt roof, then peers into the darkness.
Inside is a wooden coffin, painted red.
The lid has been smashed inward. revealing two skeletal feet.
A man. Alan Toney lifts away another stone... and freezes.
Something was done to this body... and it wasn't the work of grave robbers or casual vandals... but someone with eerie patience and a grim, singular purpose...
The man's chest cavity was pried open, his skull was severed from his spine, and his thigh bones pulled from their sockets.
Both were placed, carefully, deliberately, on top of his ruined ribcage.
Staring down into the coffin, Bellantoni realises that he isn't looking at an ordinary burial any more. but a crude skull and crossbones fashioned from human remains.
He's never seen anything like it.
I'm Tim Harford, and you're listening to Cautionary Tales.
Cautionary Tales 1883, 20 miles from Griswold, another community was facing a mystery of its own.
It began with a woman named Mary Eliza Brown.
She lived with her husband George and their seven children on the edge of the small farming settlement of Exeter, Rhode Island.
The Browns were an industrious family with a small homestead of 30 or 40 acres.
Their life followed the seasons, planting in spring, paying in summer, harvest in autumn.
In winter, when the ground froze, they hauled timber, fed and watered their animals, and waited for the thaw.
The soil in Exeter was thin, the ground stony and stubborn.
At the beginning of the century, two and a half thousand people had lived here, but by the time Mary Eliza was raising her family, fewer than a thousand remained.
Many had been drawn west by the promise of better land, and now pine and oak crowded their abandoned homesteads, reclaiming what they'd left behind.
Those who stayed coaxed cabbage and pumpkin from the soil, and grazed their livestock in rough, stone-walled pastures.
Exeter was not an easy place to live, but it was convivial.
Neighbours met at the General's store or the tavern, The local paper listed not only marriages and deaths, but ordinary everyday events.
Farming accidents, visitors to town, and who was in bed with illness.
At the white clapboard church, women organised suppers and charitable gatherings.
Everyone knew everyone's business, because everyone's business mattered.
And when trouble came to a family, it didn't belong to that family alone.
In the early 1880s, Mary Eliza began to change.
Ordinary domestic tasks such as washing and cooking left her exhausted.
Soon her clothes hung loose about her frame, and in the afternoons she grew feverish.
The Browns did what families do when someone sickens.
They watched, nursed, waited.
Eldest daughter Olive, a dressmaker, cared for her mother devotedly.
The doctors who served Exeter had seen illness like this before.
A common response was to try to strengthen the body with nourishing food, cod liver oil, fresh air and rest.
Others put their faith in patent medicines such as soothing syrups and herbal extracts.
We don't know exactly what the Browns tried, but it didn't stop Mary Eliza wasting away.
Then Olive began to flag.
That can't have been surprising at first.
She had her dressmaking work, domestic duties, and she was nursing her mother.
But soon the family noticed other changes.
She was gaunt and pale.
Her eyes appeared sunken.
At night she complained of a strange sensation, a heavy suffocating pressure on her chest.
And through it all, Mary Eliza was fading.
Just before Christmas 1883, she passed away, and her family buried her in the graveyard next to the white clapboard church.
But whatever had drained Mary Eliza did not leave with her.
Olive developed a cough, a dry, persistent racking at first, but soon her handkerchiefs came away spotted with blood, flecks of scarlet, then teaspoons.
There was a name for this kind of wasting illness, because it seemed to consume the sufferer.
It was called consumption.
Consumption was familiar in Exeter.
People knew it could pass through families, but its causes were less certain.
Some said it was hereditary.
Others blamed bad air.
Others still reached for older, stranger notions.
Perhaps something invisible was feeding on the family, moving from victim to victim.
George Brown held no truck with such beliefs.
But that didn't make what was happening to his daughter any less frightening.
Six months after her mother's death, Olive was aware that her body was failing her.
In agony and struggling to breathe, she chose a hymn for her funeral.
When Olive died in June 1884, aged 20, the whole town gathered at the church.
Together they stood to sing one sweetly solemn thought.
For the next few years, the Brown family clung to familiar routines.
The seasons turned as they always had, harvest in autumn, planting in spring.
George Brown traded in cattle, and the farm grew.
Daughter Mercy Lena, known as Lena, learnt the work of the household, sewing, mending and making do.
She also sang at the local Sunday school, along with her younger sisters, Hattie and Jenny.
Son, Eddie Brown, grew into a tall, strong young man.
He joined the local band, whose marches and polkas were the soundtrack of social life in Exeter, a favourite at fairs and lawn parties.
He helped his father in the fields, found work as a clerk at the general store, and was well-liked in the community.
When Eddie was around 21...
He got married at the local church and moved with his bride Hortense to a new house on the outskirts of town.
Shortly after the wedding, his band came to visit, filling their home with music.
Then the music faded.
Eddie Brown grew tired.
Soon he began to cough.

In 19th century New England, consumption was the leading cause of death, claiming one in four lives.
To the people of Exeter, it was terrifying and enigmatic.
Yet while they debated bad air versus bad bloodlines, science was closing in on the true culprit.
In the 1860s, French doctor Jean-Antoine Villemin proved that pulmonary tuberculosis, also known as consumption, was an infectious disease, the work of an invading pathogen.
Then in 1882, the year before Mary Eliza died, a German doctor called Robert Koch peered through his microscope and saw slender rods stained blue against the glass coverslip.
This was the tubercle bacillus. the organism behind the disease.
A monster had been feeding on the brown family.
It wasn't invisible, but it was very, very small, and now it could be studied.

Koch's discovery was a major victory for germ theory, but his findings were still new, and while they'd made their way to New England, they hadn't yet filtered through every town, let alone every farmhouse.
Still, By the time Eddie Brown fell sick, doctors had a better idea of what they were dealing with.
Open windows, rest and a warm climate had long been prescribed for consumption.
Now these remedies carried a new scientific logic.
If something infectious was passing between people, fresh, moving air might help keep it at bay.
Doctors advised their patients to go to the mountains, where the air was clean and the climate sunny and dry.
Brochures invited the sick to the land of new lungs, imploring them to come west and live.
In California and Colorado, cities filled with so-called lungers.
In the Adirondacks and other mountain resorts, specialised sanatoria were opened.
Here, patients spent as much time as possible outside, resting in the open air.
A number of them reported that their symptoms eased.
They seemed to get better.
George Brown had faced consumption twice before.
First in his wife, then in his eldest daughter.
He'd buried them both.
And now his son was sick.
Eddie was 22, married, and making his own way in the world.
A journey to the mountains would mean leaving his loved ones, his work, and the family farm.
But in the end, the Browns decided it was worth it.
In the autumn of 1890, he set out for Colorado Springs.
Eddie probably travelled by train, watching the green hills of New England give way to vast, flat prairies. until the Rocky Mountains rose on the horizon.
When he arrived, it wasn't into untouched wilderness, but a young city, crawling with people who were all there for the same reason, to get well.
Many of them stayed in boarding houses with special porches for consumptives to sleep in.
Others stayed outside in canvas tents.
Eddie settled among them.
A few months later, his wife Hortense followed him, chaperoned by his trusty former employer.
Together, Hortense's care and the Colorado climate seemed to work their magic.
The color returned to Eddie's cheeks, and his frail frame gradually filled out again.
His cough persisted, but he was well enough to take up work as a conductor on the city's streetcars.
News of Eddie's happy improvement reached Exeter.
For the Browns and their friends, it was something to celebrate.
But their joy was tempered.
Eddie's sister, Lena, was fading fast.
Lena's health troubles had started in the summer of 1890, just before Eddie left home.
It's unclear why she didn't go with her brother to Colorado.
There may only have been enough money for one of the Browns to make the long journey, or she may have been deemed too weak to travel.
In any case, Lena stayed in Exeter, and by November 1891, the local illness log described her condition as very critical.
George Brown called in a local physician, Dr Harold Metcalf, widely regarded as one of the best doctors in the area.
He'd worked for some years at New York City's Bellevue Hospital, attending patients on the horse-drawn aid wagons that raced through the streets each day.
He was experienced and pragmatic, but the doctor examined Lena and told her father George that there was nothing he could do to save her.
He could make her comfortable.
Doctors used morphine and opium to quiet coughing and soothe pain.
But by this stage, Lena's lungs were badly damaged.
She was 19 years old.
On a bitter midwinter day, George Brown laid a second daughter to rest beside his wife.
The ground outside was frozen hard.
Lena was placed in a crypt in the churchyard, where she would remain until the spring thaw.
A month after Lena was buried, Eddie and Hortense returned to Exeter, not because Eddie had been restored to full health, but because he'd taken a turn for the worse.
The Colorado climate no longer seemed able to help him.
He managed the long journey, but arrived in Rhode Island exhausted.
Eddie was genuinely beloved in his hometown, and the local paper reflected that affection.
If the good wishes and prayers of his many friends could be realised, friend Eddie would be speedily restored to perfect health.
Some of Eddie's neighbours thought they knew how to make those prayers come true.
There was an old supernatural remedy, something George Brown hadn't tried yet, and they believed it might save his son.
Local law held that when consumption swept through a family, it wasn't just an illness, it was the dead reaching back from beyond the grave to drain the living.
If this was what was happening to Eddie, then there was only one way to stop the feeding.
Go to the churchyard, open the graves of Mary Eliza, Olive and Lena, and destroy the source.
The neighbours approached George and asked for permission to take the necessary steps.
He must have understood their desperation. but he could not grant their terrible request.
Griswold, Connecticut, 1991.
After a year of excavation, Nick Bellantoni and his team had found the remains of 29 people.

The burial ground had been a small farm cemetery where generations of families had been laid to rest side by side The skeleton from the crypt the one that had been carefully arranged into a skull and crossbones came to be known as JB because JB55 had been spelled out in brass tacks on his coffin lid Bellantoni sent JB to the National Museum of Health and Medicine,
Washington DC, where investigations revealed that he'd died in the early 19th century, aged around 55.
He'd suffered from arthritis and something else too.
All over his ribs were pale, pitted lesions, evidence of a chronic pulmonary infection that likely caused chest pain and coughing.
JB had almost certainly died of tuberculosis.
What's more, forensic examination showed that when JB was rearranged, there'd been no flesh left on his bones.
His body was already fully decomposed.
Whatever the skull and crossbones ritual was, it hadn't taken place around the time of his death.
Instead, it had been performed at least five years later.
Bellantoni knew that he was looking at some kind of ritual and to help him decipher what it meant, he reached out to folklorist Michael Bell.
Bell had spent years researching strange disturbances to burial grounds all over New England in the 18th and 19th centuries and he told Bellantoni that he'd observed a distinct pattern.
When consumption decimated a family, people sometimes returned to the dead and opened their graves.
They weren't looking for loot.
They were looking for something else.
In Exeter, 1892, Eddie Brown grew ever weaker.
He and his family knew the disease was doing its final work.
In the morning, he woke drenched from night sweats.
Every cough tore at his chest and as his lungs filled with blood and pus, even the simple act of drawing breath was a struggle.
The people of Exeter came to George again and repeated their request.
This time George spoke with his son Eddie.
Then he went back to his neighbours and gave his consent.
A group of men gathered at the graves of Mary Eliza, Olive and Lena, shovels in hand.
Cautionary Tales will be back shortly.
In March 1892...
Dr Harold Metcalf opened his door to an agitated young man.
Eddie Brown was in a dying condition, he said, and a number of Exeter townsmen had exhumed the body of Mary Eliza Brown in order to save him.
He wanted Metcalf to come and examine her remains.
Then he muttered something else, something about blood and dead family members returning to feed on the living.
Absurd, said the doctor.
He was a man of science, and though he hadn't treated Eddie Brown, he knew that Eddie's sister Lena had died of pulmonary tuberculosis.
There was no mystery to be found in any of the Brown graves.
He turned the messenger away.
Before long, the young man was back, and this time he carried word from George Brown.
The farmer was clear that he didn't believe in any superstition himself, but he wanted Metcalfe to dissect the bodies of his dead wife and daughters all the same.
Metcalfe was baffled, but he agreed.
He gathered his instruments and set out.
At the churchyard, a group of men were waiting beside an open grave.
Metcalfe saw that Mary Eliza had already been dug up.
Her remains were withered and shrunken by years underground.
George and Eddie were nowhere to be seen.
But among the men present was a journalist from the Providence Journal.
Later, he described Mary Eliza's body as mummified.
Then men had summoned Metcalfe to look for liquid blood, the supposed link between the dead and the living.
He watched as they set their shovels to a second grave, olive brown.
But when the coffin lid was pried open, there was nothing left to examine, only dry bones and a lingering shock of hair.
That left Lina.
Unlike her mother and sister, Lina had not been interred in the ground.
Instead, she'd been placed in a cold stone crypt to wait out the winter.
The men now opened it and were astonished by what they saw.
Two months after her death, Lina had changed remarkably little.
Her skin and flesh were still intact.
Metcalfe followed his instructions.
He stepped forward with his scalpel, made a careful incision into Lina's torso and removed her heart.
He laid the organ out, and sliced into the muscle.
And then they saw it.
A chilling streak of red.
Liquid blood. Metcalfe knew that there was nothing supernatural about this, and he tried to explain that the lack of decomposition to Lena's body was normal.
She'd only been dead for two months, and she'd been kept in the cold.
He also pointed to her lungs, which were riddled with scar tissue.
But the townsmen had found what they were looking for, blood in the heart of a woman who died of consumption.
To them, this was evidence that some part of Lena Brown was undead and leeching life from her brother.
There was an obvious problem with this story.
Mary, Eliza and Olive had died long before Lena had even fallen ill.
She couldn't have been feeding on them.
But perhaps that mattered less than the fact that Eddie was still alive and wasting away, and now there was something they could do about it.
The old belief held that as long as blood remained in the heart of the dead person, their family members would continue to die.
And so... There in the churchyard, the men kindled a fire, cast Lena's heart into the flames and watched it burn to ash.
According to the ritual, Eddie Brown was supposed to drink those ashes mixed into a tonic.
We don't know if he ever did.
In 2019... Nearly 30 years after Nick Bellantoni unearthed JB, researchers were finally able to narrow down who he might have been.
Using DNA profiling and genealogical records, they concluded that he'd probably been a farmer named John Barber, who'd lived in the area in the 1800s.
Close to JB, the team had found another, smaller coffin marked NB13. almost certainly Barber's son, Nathan, who had died as a young teenager.
Ballantoni theorised that the skull and crossbones ritual was an apotropaic remedy, that is, a kind of magic intended to ward off evil.
Similar practices have been observed in Europe.
Across the Atlantic, corpses were sometimes found bloated, with their hair and fingernails apparently still growing, and blood in the heart and chest cavity.
All these things had natural explanations, but to people who didn't understand the processes of decomposition, they could look like signs that the dead were not quite finished with the living.
By the time someone came for John Barber, there was no heart left to examine.
His soft tissue had disappeared.
And so whoever returned to his grave chose another old practice intended to stop the dead returning.
They separated his skull and his legs from his body.
Years later, in 1896, 1892, Lena Brown became the focus of the same desperate hope.
The story was eerily captivating, so much so that it even crossed the Atlantic.
In 1912, a newspaper clipping detailing Lena's exhumation was found tucked away among the posthumous personal papers of the author of Dracula, one Bram Stoker.
The Providence Journal covered the exhumation ritual with a sneer, sensationalising it as a lurid vampire panic.
It's not clear that anyone in Exeter actually used the word vampire or believed that this is what they were dealing with.
All the same, the newspaper used gothic tropes to mock the townsfolk as ignorant bumpkins who preferred superstition to science.
I think the picture is far messier and far more human.
True, the people who opened Lena's grave didn't understand tuberculosis as their doctors did.
True, their explanation was magical.
But that doesn't mean their decision was a simple contest between science and superstition.
Koch had found the bacillus, that was one thing.
But learning how to diagnose tuberculosis, prevent its spread, treat it, and eventually cure it, would take decades, and far more than scientific discovery.
It demanded public health systems, better housing, sanitation, new nursing practices, education and millions of tiny changes in everyday behaviour.
The Brown family lived in the long gap between science understanding what was killing people and science knowing how to stop it.
On paper, George Brown's decision to allow the exhumation to go ahead looks like a contradiction.
He was a pragmatic farmer who sought out modern doctors, sent his son west, and insisted that he had no faith in the old folk beliefs.
Yet, he gave his consent anyway.
Exeter was a small, tightly connected place, and that probably played a role in his decisions.
Neighbours read about the bed bound in the local paper and watched over the sick.
They helped with farm work, celebrated marriages, and gathered for funerals.

George might have found some of their beliefs strange, but these were people he knew, people he relied on, and people he would have to live alongside after Eddie was gone, if Eddie was gone. but I wonder if something else was at work here too.
Medical sociologists sometimes talk about a form of action bias called the treatment imperative.
This is the pressure to keep treating a patient who's dying, even when the intervention carries a high burden of distress, and even when the chance of success is vanishingly small.
Doctors can feel it, patients can feel it, and families can feel it too, The very existence of an intervention can create the powerful sense that it ought to be tried.
This idea is usually associated with modern medicine and its technological advances.
George Brown didn't have an intensive care unit full of machines or an arsenal of drugs.
All the same, I think the treatment imperative can help illuminate the dilemma he faced.
To George, doing nothing may have felt less like the simple absence of action and more like a deliberate choice to let his son die.
The ritual offered him what medicine could not, something he could do.
Perhaps the question was no longer, do I believe this will work?
And instead became, can I live with myself if I don't try?
In May 1892, two months after the exhumation, George Brown buried his son.
Eddie was 24 years old.
His obituary described him as a young man of sterling integrity and someone that any community could ill afford to lose, with a white clapboard church filled for his funeral.
A local weaving shop sent cushions bearing the words... husband and shopmate.
The casket was covered in flowers, including a wreath from his old employer with the inscription, Loved Ones Parted, and a choir sang the hymn, Some Sweet Day.
George Brown had lost his wife and three children.
He would go on to bury three more daughters, Annie, Jenny and Myra, Only Hattie survived him.
He lived in Exeter for another 30 years, side by side with the same neighbours who'd opened the graves of his wife and daughters to try and save his son.
In that time, the world transformed.
The X-ray opened a window into the human body and scientists developed the first tuberculosis vaccine.
But in May 1892...
None of that existed yet.
At Eddie's funeral, the choir sang of a different kind of hope.
By and by, some sweet day, we shall meet our loved ones gone.

George Brown traded in cattle, and the farm grew. Daughter Mercy Lena, known as Lena, learnt the work of the household, sewing, mending and making do. She also sang at the local Sunday school, along with her younger sisters, Hattie and Jenny. Son, Eddie Brown, grew into a tall, strong young man.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: He joined the local band, whose marches and polkas were the soundtrack of social life in Exeter, a favourite at fairs and lawn parties. He helped his father in the fields, found work as a clerk at the general store, and was well-liked in the community. When Eddie was around 21... He got married at the local church and moved with his bride Hortense to a new house on the outskirts of town.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Shortly after the wedding, his band came to visit, filling their home with music. Then the music faded. Eddie Brown grew tired. Soon he began to cough. Cautionary Tales will return. In 19th century New England, consumption was the leading cause of death, claiming one in four lives. To the people of Exeter, it was terrifying and enigmatic. Yet while they debated bad air versus bad bloodlines, science was closing in on the true culprit.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: In the 1860s, French doctor Jean-Antoine Villemin proved that pulmonary tuberculosis, also known as consumption, was an infectious disease, the work of an invading pathogen. Then in 1882, the year before Mary Eliza died, a German doctor called Robert Koch peered through his microscope and saw slender rods stained blue against the glass coverslip. This was the tubercle bacillus. the organism behind the disease. A monster had been feeding on the brown family.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: It wasn't invisible, but it was very, very small, and now it could be studied. Koch's discovery was a major victory for germ theory, but his findings were still new, and while they'd made their way to New England, they hadn't yet filtered through every town, let alone every farmhouse. Still, By the time Eddie Brown fell sick, doctors had a better idea of what they were dealing with. Open windows, rest and a warm climate had long been prescribed for consumption.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Now these remedies carried a new scientific logic. If something infectious was passing between people, fresh, moving air might help keep it at bay. Doctors advised their patients to go to the mountains, where the air was clean and the climate sunny and dry. Brochures invited the sick to the land of new lungs, imploring them to come west and live. In California and Colorado, cities filled with so-called lungers.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: In the Adirondacks and other mountain resorts, specialised sanatoria were opened. Here, patients spent as much time as possible outside, resting in the open air. A number of them reported that their symptoms eased. They seemed to get better. George Brown had faced consumption twice before. First in his wife, then in his eldest daughter. He'd buried them both. And now his son was sick. Eddie was 22, married, and making his own way in the world.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: A journey to the mountains would mean leaving his loved ones, his work, and the family farm. But in the end, the Browns decided it was worth it. In the autumn of 1890, he set out for Colorado Springs. Eddie probably travelled by train, watching the green hills of New England give way to vast, flat prairies. until the Rocky Mountains rose on the horizon.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: When he arrived, it wasn't into untouched wilderness, but a young city, crawling with people who were all there for the same reason, to get well. Many of them stayed in boarding houses with special porches for consumptives to sleep in. Others stayed outside in canvas tents. Eddie settled among them. A few months later, his wife Hortense followed him, chaperoned by his trusty former employer. Together, Hortense's care and the Colorado climate seemed to work their magic.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: The color returned to Eddie's cheeks, and his frail frame gradually filled out again. His cough persisted, but he was well enough to take up work as a conductor on the city's streetcars. News of Eddie's happy improvement reached Exeter. For the Browns and their friends, it was something to celebrate. But their joy was tempered. Eddie's sister, Lena, was fading fast. Lena's health troubles had started in the summer of 1890, just before Eddie left home.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: It's unclear why she didn't go with her brother to Colorado. There may only have been enough money for one of the Browns to make the long journey, or she may have been deemed too weak to travel. In any case, Lena stayed in Exeter, and by November 1891, the local illness log described her condition as very critical.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: George Brown called in a local physician, Dr Harold Metcalf, widely regarded as one of the best doctors in the area. He'd worked for some years at New York City's Bellevue Hospital, attending patients on the horse-drawn aid wagons that raced through the streets each day. He was experienced and pragmatic, but the doctor examined Lena and told her father George that there was nothing he could do to save her.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: He could make her comfortable. Doctors used morphine and opium to quiet coughing and soothe pain. But by this stage, Lena's lungs were badly damaged. She was 19 years old. On a bitter midwinter day, George Brown laid a second daughter to rest beside his wife. The ground outside was frozen hard. Lena was placed in a crypt in the churchyard, where she would remain until the spring thaw. A month after Lena was buried, Eddie and Hortense returned to Exeter, not because Eddie had been restored to full health, but because he'd taken a turn for the worse.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: The Colorado climate no longer seemed able to help him. He managed the long journey, but arrived in Rhode Island exhausted. Eddie was genuinely beloved in his hometown, and the local paper reflected that affection. If the good wishes and prayers of his many friends could be realised, friend Eddie would be speedily restored to perfect health. Some of Eddie's neighbours thought they knew how to make those prayers come true.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: There was an old supernatural remedy, something George Brown hadn't tried yet, and they believed it might save his son. Local law held that when consumption swept through a family, it wasn't just an illness, it was the dead reaching back from beyond the grave to drain the living. If this was what was happening to Eddie, then there was only one way to stop the feeding. Go to the churchyard, open the graves of Mary Eliza, Olive and Lena, and destroy the source.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: The neighbours approached George and asked for permission to take the necessary steps. He must have understood their desperation. but he could not grant their terrible request. Griswold, Connecticut, 1991. After a year of excavation, Nick Bellantoni and his team had found the remains of 29 people. The burial ground had been a small farm cemetery where generations of families had been laid to rest side by side The skeleton from the crypt the one that had been carefully arranged into a skull and crossbones came to be known as JB because JB55 had been spelled out in brass tacks on his coffin lid Bellantoni sent JB to the National Museum of Health and Medicine, Washington DC, where investigations revealed that he'd died in the early 19th century, aged around 55.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: He'd suffered from arthritis and something else too. All over his ribs were pale, pitted lesions, evidence of a chronic pulmonary infection that likely caused chest pain and coughing. JB had almost certainly died of tuberculosis. What's more, forensic examination showed that when JB was rearranged, there'd been no flesh left on his bones. His body was already fully decomposed. Whatever the skull and crossbones ritual was, it hadn't taken place around the time of his death.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Instead, it had been performed at least five years later. Bellantoni knew that he was looking at some kind of ritual and to help him decipher what it meant, he reached out to folklorist Michael Bell. Bell had spent years researching strange disturbances to burial grounds all over New England in the 18th and 19th centuries and he told Bellantoni that he'd observed a distinct pattern. When consumption decimated a family, people sometimes returned to the dead and opened their graves.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: They weren't looking for loot. They were looking for something else. In Exeter, 1892, Eddie Brown grew ever weaker. He and his family knew the disease was doing its final work. In the morning, he woke drenched from night sweats. Every cough tore at his chest and as his lungs filled with blood and pus, even the simple act of drawing breath was a struggle. The people of Exeter came to George again and repeated their request.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: This time George spoke with his son Eddie. Then he went back to his neighbours and gave his consent.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: A group of men gathered at the graves of Mary Eliza, Olive and Lena, shovels in hand. Cautionary Tales will be back shortly. In March 1892... Dr Harold Metcalf opened his door to an agitated young man. Eddie Brown was in a dying condition, he said, and a number of Exeter townsmen had exhumed the body of Mary Eliza Brown in order to save him. He wanted Metcalf to come and examine her remains.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Then he muttered something else, something about blood and dead family members returning to feed on the living. Absurd, said the doctor. He was a man of science, and though he hadn't treated Eddie Brown, he knew that Eddie's sister Lena had died of pulmonary tuberculosis. There was no mystery to be found in any of the Brown graves. He turned the messenger away. Before long, the young man was back, and this time he carried word from George Brown.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: The farmer was clear that he didn't believe in any superstition himself, but he wanted Metcalfe to dissect the bodies of his dead wife and daughters all the same. Metcalfe was baffled, but he agreed. He gathered his instruments and set out. At the churchyard, a group of men were waiting beside an open grave. Metcalfe saw that Mary Eliza had already been dug up. Her remains were withered and shrunken by years underground.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: George and Eddie were nowhere to be seen. But among the men present was a journalist from the Providence Journal. Later, he described Mary Eliza's body as mummified. Then men had summoned Metcalfe to look for liquid blood, the supposed link between the dead and the living.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: He watched as they set their shovels to a second grave, olive brown. But when the coffin lid was pried open, there was nothing left to examine, only dry bones and a lingering shock of hair. That left Lina. Unlike her mother and sister, Lina had not been interred in the ground. Instead, she'd been placed in a cold stone crypt to wait out the winter. The men now opened it and were astonished by what they saw.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Two months after her death, Lina had changed remarkably little. Her skin and flesh were still intact. Metcalfe followed his instructions. He stepped forward with his scalpel, made a careful incision into Lina's torso and removed her heart. He laid the organ out, and sliced into the muscle. And then they saw it. A chilling streak of red. Liquid blood. Metcalfe knew that there was nothing supernatural about this, and he tried to explain that the lack of decomposition to Lena's body was normal.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: She'd only been dead for two months, and she'd been kept in the cold. He also pointed to her lungs, which were riddled with scar tissue. But the townsmen had found what they were looking for, blood in the heart of a woman who died of consumption. To them, this was evidence that some part of Lena Brown was undead and leeching life from her brother. There was an obvious problem with this story.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Mary, Eliza and Olive had died long before Lena had even fallen ill. She couldn't have been feeding on them. But perhaps that mattered less than the fact that Eddie was still alive and wasting away, and now there was something they could do about it. The old belief held that as long as blood remained in the heart of the dead person, their family members would continue to die.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And so... There in the churchyard, the men kindled a fire, cast Lena's heart into the flames and watched it burn to ash. According to the ritual, Eddie Brown was supposed to drink those ashes mixed into a tonic. We don't know if he ever did. In 2019... Nearly 30 years after Nick Bellantoni unearthed JB, researchers were finally able to narrow down who he might have been. Using DNA profiling and genealogical records, they concluded that he'd probably been a farmer named John Barber, who'd lived in the area in the 1800s.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Close to JB, the team had found another, smaller coffin marked NB13. almost certainly Barber's son, Nathan, who had died as a young teenager. Ballantoni theorised that the skull and crossbones ritual was an apotropaic remedy, that is, a kind of magic intended to ward off evil. Similar practices have been observed in Europe. Across the Atlantic, corpses were sometimes found bloated, with their hair and fingernails apparently still growing, and blood in the heart and chest cavity.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: All these things had natural explanations, but to people who didn't understand the processes of decomposition, they could look like signs that the dead were not quite finished with the living.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: By the time someone came for John Barber, there was no heart left to examine. His soft tissue had disappeared. And so whoever returned to his grave chose another old practice intended to stop the dead returning. They separated his skull and his legs from his body. Years later, in 1896, 1892, Lena Brown became the focus of the same desperate hope. The story was eerily captivating, so much so that it even crossed the Atlantic.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: In 1912, a newspaper clipping detailing Lena's exhumation was found tucked away among the posthumous personal papers of the author of Dracula, one Bram Stoker. The Providence Journal covered the exhumation ritual with a sneer, sensationalising it as a lurid vampire panic. It's not clear that anyone in Exeter actually used the word vampire or believed that this is what they were dealing with. All the same, the newspaper used gothic tropes to mock the townsfolk as ignorant bumpkins who preferred superstition to science.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: I think the picture is far messier and far more human. True, the people who opened Lena's grave didn't understand tuberculosis as their doctors did. True, their explanation was magical. But that doesn't mean their decision was a simple contest between science and superstition. Koch had found the bacillus, that was one thing. But learning how to diagnose tuberculosis, prevent its spread, treat it, and eventually cure it, would take decades, and far more than scientific discovery.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: It demanded public health systems, better housing, sanitation, new nursing practices, education and millions of tiny changes in everyday behaviour. The Brown family lived in the long gap between science understanding what was killing people and science knowing how to stop it. On paper, George Brown's decision to allow the exhumation to go ahead looks like a contradiction. He was a pragmatic farmer who sought out modern doctors, sent his son west, and insisted that he had no faith in the old folk beliefs.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Yet, he gave his consent anyway. Exeter was a small, tightly connected place, and that probably played a role in his decisions. Neighbours read about the bed bound in the local paper and watched over the sick. They helped with farm work, celebrated marriages, and gathered for funerals. George might have found some of their beliefs strange, but these were people he knew, people he relied on, and people he would have to live alongside after Eddie was gone, if Eddie was gone. but I wonder if something else was at work here too.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Medical sociologists sometimes talk about a form of action bias called the treatment imperative. This is the pressure to keep treating a patient who's dying, even when the intervention carries a high burden of distress, and even when the chance of success is vanishingly small. Doctors can feel it, patients can feel it, and families can feel it too, The very existence of an intervention can create the powerful sense that it ought to be tried.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: This idea is usually associated with modern medicine and its technological advances. George Brown didn't have an intensive care unit full of machines or an arsenal of drugs. All the same, I think the treatment imperative can help illuminate the dilemma he faced. To George, doing nothing may have felt less like the simple absence of action and more like a deliberate choice to let his son die. The ritual offered him what medicine could not, something he could do.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Perhaps the question was no longer, do I believe this will work? And instead became, can I live with myself if I don't try? In May 1892, two months after the exhumation, George Brown buried his son. Eddie was 24 years old. His obituary described him as a young man of sterling integrity and someone that any community could ill afford to lose, with a white clapboard church filled for his funeral.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: A local weaving shop sent cushions bearing the words... husband and shopmate. The casket was covered in flowers, including a wreath from his old employer with the inscription, Loved Ones Parted, and a choir sang the hymn, Some Sweet Day. George Brown had lost his wife and three children. He would go on to bury three more daughters, Annie, Jenny and Myra, Only Hattie survived him. He lived in Exeter for another 30 years, side by side with the same neighbours who'd opened the graves of his wife and daughters to try and save his son.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: In that time, the world transformed. The X-ray opened a window into the human body and scientists developed the first tuberculosis vaccine. But in May 1892... None of that existed yet. At Eddie's funeral, the choir sang of a different kind of hope. By and by, some sweet day, we shall meet our loved ones gone. Some sweet day, by and by.

study.one_liner_ko: 1890년대 로드아일랜드 엑시터에서 결핵으로 가족을 잃어가던 조지 브라운이 왜 '흡혈귀 의식'에 동의했는지를, 과학과 미신의 이분법이 아니라 '치료 충동(treatment imperative)'으로 설명하는 에피소드.
summary_ko: 1990년 코네티컷의 자갈 채취장에서 아이들이 해골을 발견하고, 주 고고학자 벨란토니가 해골과 대퇴골을 가슴 위에 X자로 배열한 기이한 무덤(JB)을 발굴한다.
1883년부터 엑시터의 브라운 가족은 어머니 메리 엘리자, 딸 올리브, 딸 레나가 차례로 결핵(당시 이름은 consumption)으로 죽는 일을 겪는다. 이때 코흐가 결핵균을 발견했지만 그 지식은 아직 시골 농가까지 퍼지지 않았다.
아들 에디는 요양을 위해 콜로라도로 갔다가 상태가 악화되어 돌아온다. 이웃들은 죽은 가족이 산 사람의 생기를 빨아먹는다는 옛 믿음에 따라 무덤을 열자고 요구한다.
1892년 3월 마을 사람들은 무덤을 파헤친다. 두 달밖에 안 된 레나의 심장에서 액체 상태의 피가 나오자 그 심장을 태우고, 재를 에디에게 마시게 하려 한다. 의사 메트칼프는 이것이 자연스러운 현상이라고 설명했지만 소용이 없었다.
2019년 연구자들은 JB가 농부 존 바버였을 가능성이 높다고 밝힌다. 이 의식은 유럽에도 있던 악을 막는 주술(apotropaic)이었다. 언론은 이를 '흡혈귀 소동'이라며 조롱했고, 이 기사는 브램 스토커의 서류 속에서도 발견됐다.
하포드는 이 일을 과학 대 미신의 단순한 대결로 보지 않는다. 과학이 병의 원인을 아는 것과 치료법을 아는 것 사이에는 긴 공백이 있었다. 조지는 '아무것도 안 하는 것'이 아들을 죽게 내버려두는 선택처럼 느껴지는 치료 충동 때문에 동의했을 수 있다고 본다.
study.summary_en: This Cautionary Tales episode starts with kids finding a skull in a Connecticut gravel pit, which leads to a strange grave where the bones were arranged like a skull and crossbones. Then it jumps to 1880s Exeter, Rhode Island, where tuberculosis killed the Brown family one by one. Koch had just found the bacterium, but nobody had a cure. When the son Eddie got worse, the neighbours wanted to dig up the dead and burn the heart of his sister Lena. The father didn't believe it, but he said yes anyway. Harford's point is that it wasn't science versus superstition. It was the treatment imperative: can I live with myself if I don't try?

I feel cautious optimism about the deal.

expressions.quote: dissect the bodies of his dead wife and daughters all the same
expressions.nuance_ko: 앞 내용과 모순되는 행동이나 결과를 이어 말할 때 쓴다. 문장 끝이나 문두에 둘 수 있고, 'still', 'even so'보다 구어체이면서 부드럽다.
examples: I told him it wouldn't work, but he tried it all the same.
It's a long shot. All the same, let's apply.
I didn't need a gift, but thanks all the same.

similar.example: It was expensive. Even so, we bought it.
The plan was risky; nonetheless, they went ahead.

expressions.expression: True, X. But that doesn't mean Y.
expressions.quote: True, their explanation was magical. But that doesn't mean their decision
expressions.meaning_ko: 맞다, X다. 하지만 그렇다고 Y는 아니다 (양보 후 반박)
expressions.nuance_ko: 상대 주장의 일부를 인정한 뒤 결론으로의 비약을 막는 토론용 구조다. 공정해 보이면서 반박이 설득력을 얻는다. 패널이나 회의에서 쓰기 좋다.
examples: True, the launch slipped. But that doesn't mean the product is a failure.
True, he's blunt. But that doesn't mean he's wrong.
True, prices are up. But that doesn't mean the economy is collapsing.

similar.example: Granted, it's expensive, but it'll last a decade.
That said, I wouldn't rule it out.

expressions.expression: the picture is far messier than that
expressions.quote: I think the picture is far messier and far more human.
expressions.nuance_ko: 깔끔한 이분법적 서사를 반박할 때 쓴다. 'I think the picture is more X'로 의견을 부드럽게 제시한다. 토론에서 단순화에 반박하는 아주 유용한 틀이다.
examples: People say it's all about talent, but I think the picture is far messier.
The headline says layoffs hit morale, but the picture is more complicated.
It's not a simple good-versus-bad story. The picture is messier and more human.

similar.example: It's more nuanced than that, honestly.
It's not black and white.

expressions.quote: a form of action bias called the treatment imperative
expressions.meaning_ko: 행동 편향: 효과가 불확실해도 뭔가 해야 한다고 느끼는 성향
expressions.nuance_ko: 행동경제학 용어로, 가만히 있는 것보다 뭐라도 하는 쪽이 낫다고 느끼는 경향이다. 축구 골키퍼, 투자, 의료 등에서 자주 논의된다. 'a form of X called Y' 정의 방식도 함께 배울 만하다.
examples: Selling in a panic is classic action bias.
The team has an action bias. They'd rather do something than wait for data.
Goalkeepers dive because of action bias, even though staying put is often better.

similar.example: Startups often prize a bias for action.

similar.expression: do something for the sake of it
similar.example: Don't do something just for the sake of it.

expressions.quote: the chance of success is vanishingly small
expressions.nuance_ko: 확률, 가능성, 차이 등이 거의 0에 가깝다고 강조한다. 'vanishingly rare/unlikely/small'로 자주 쓰며 격식 있고 분석적인 뉴스나 토론 어조다.
examples: The odds of winning the lottery are vanishingly small.
Realistically, the chance of a rate cut this quarter is vanishingly small.
The difference between the two phones is vanishingly small.

similar.example: We got next to nothing for the old car.
His chances are slim to none.

expressions.expression: less like X and more like Y
expressions.quote: less like the simple absence of action and more like a deliberate choice
expressions.nuance_ko: 같은 사실을 다른 프레임으로 재해석할 때 쓴다. 'felt less like X and more like Y'가 흔하며, 감정이나 인식을 설명할 때 좋다. 틀짓기가 필요한 발언에 유용하다.
examples: The meeting felt less like a discussion and more like a performance.
Moving abroad felt less like an escape and more like a fresh start.
The new policy is less like a fix and more like a bandage.

similar.example: It was more a lecture than a conversation.
It felt like an opportunity rather than a risk.

expressions.expression: can I live with myself if I don't try?
expressions.quote: can I live with myself if I don't try?
expressions.meaning_ko: 시도하지 않으면 스스로를 용서할 수 있을까 (양심의 기준)
expressions.nuance_ko: 'live with oneself'는 자기 행동에 대한 죄책감이나 양심을 견딜 수 있느냐는 뜻이다. 도덕적, 감정적 판단 기준을 말할 때 쓴다. 'I couldn't live with myself if...'가 가장 흔한 형태다.
examples: I couldn't live with myself if I stayed quiet about the mistake.
Can you live with yourself after what you said to her?
If I don't at least apply, I won't be able to live with myself.

similar.example: How can you sleep at night after cutting corners?
I couldn't face myself in the mirror if I'd lied.

expressions.quote: someone that any community could ill afford to lose
expressions.meaning_ko: ~할 여유가 거의 없다, 잃으면 큰 타격이다
expressions.nuance_ko: 금전 여유뿐 아니라 인재나 시간, 평판을 잃으면 안 되는 상황을 말할 때 쓴다. 'can ill afford + to V / 명사' 형태이며 격식 있다.
examples: We can ill afford another delay on this project.
The team could ill afford to lose its best engineer.
In this market, we can ill afford a bad hire.

similar.example: We can't afford to wait.
We have little room for error.

expressions.nuance_ko: 폭풍, 불황, 위기처럼 지나가기만 기다려야 하는 상황에 쓴다. 능동적으로 해결하지 않고 지나가길 기다린다는 느낌이다. 'wait out the storm/market'이 대표적이다.
examples: We waited out the rain in a café.
Some investors just wait out the downturn instead of selling.
He's hoping to wait out the scandal and keep his job.

similar.example: The company managed to ride out the recession.
Sit tight until we hear back.

expressions.quote: researchers were finally able to narrow down who he might have been
expressions.nuance_ko: 후보나 선택지의 범위를 줄일 때 쓴다. 'narrow it down to + 수' 형태로 많이 쓴다. 회의나 일상에서 모두 자연스러운 필수 표현이다.
examples: We've narrowed the candidates down to three.
Can you narrow down the time when it crashed?
I'm trying to narrow down where to go for the holidays.

similar.example: We whittled the list down to five.
They shortlisted two applicants.

expressions.quote: a kind of magic intended to ward off evil
expressions.nuance_ko: 나쁜 일이 일어나지 않게 막는다는 뜻이다. 미신(ward off evil)부터 'ward off a cold, a takeover bid'까지 폭넓게 쓴다. 'keep at bay'보다 방어 행위에 초점이 있다.
examples: I take vitamin C every winter to ward off colds.
The company adopted a poison pill to ward off a takeover.
She wore a lucky charm to ward off bad luck.

similar.example: He fended off criticism from the press.
A coffee might stave off the afternoon slump.

vocab.example: The shopping cart careened down the parking lot.
Police cordoned off the street after the accident.
It was a convivial dinner with old friends.
By the third hour of the meeting, everyone was flagging.
He looked gaunt after weeks of flu.
She gave an enigmatic smile and said nothing.
The old sanatorium in the hills is now a hotel.
The storm decimated the town's tourism season.
Authorities exhumed the body for a second autopsy.
He was interred in the family plot.
The company severed ties with its supplier.
Many cultures hang apotropaic charms above doorways.
The tabloids ran a lurid account of the scandal.
He was treated like a country bumpkin at the party.
She received a posthumous award for her work.
I coaxed the cat out from under the sofa.

warmup.q: Have you ever done something you didn't really believe in, just because it felt better than doing nothing?
warmup.hint_ko: 병원, 투자, 직장에서 '일단 해보자'고 했던 개인 경험과 그 이유(불안, 책임감)를 말해 보세요.

warmup.q: What's a superstition or folk remedy from your culture that people still follow?
warmup.hint_ko: 한국의 속설이나 민간요법, 사례와 사람들이 왜 아직 믿는지를 설명해 보세요.

opinion.q: Do you think it's fair to call the people of Exeter ignorant? Why or why not?
opinion.hint_ko: 당시 과학의 한계, 공동체 압력, 현대에도 비슷한 비합리적 결정이 있는지 연결해 보세요.

opinion.q: Where do you see 'action bias' or the treatment imperative today, in medicine, business or politics?
opinion.hint_ko: 기업의 무리한 구조조정, 과잉 진료, 정책의 보여주기식 대응 등 구체적 사례를 들어보세요.

debate.q: When a family is facing a hopeless situation, is it right to allow harmless but unproven rituals or treatments?
debate.for: 해가 없고 가족에게 심리적 위안과 '할 만큼 했다'는 마음을 준다. 환자의 자율성과 공동체의 정서도 존중해야 한다.
debate.against: 가짜 희망은 실제 치료를 미루게 하고, 시신 훼손처럼 해가 되는 경우도 있다. 사실을 정직하게 알리는 것이 더 윤리적이다.

debate.q: Should the media mock beliefs it considers irrational, as the Providence Journal did?
debate.for: 잘못된 믿음을 방치하면 공중보건에 위험하고, 비판적 사고를 촉진할 수 있다.
debate.against: 조롱은 사람들을 방어적으로 만들고 맥락(과학 지식의 공백)을 무시한다. 이해와 공감이 설득에 더 효과적이다.

roleplay.scenario: A close friend's elderly parent is seriously ill, and the friend is considering an expensive, unproven overseas treatment. You are talking over coffee.
roleplay.your_role: A caring friend who is skeptical but doesn't want to hurt your friend
roleplay.partner_role: The friend who feels they must try everything
goals: Acknowledge their feelings with a concession like 'True, ... but that doesn't mean...'
Use at least two expressions from the episode (e.g. 'live with myself', 'all the same', 'vanishingly small')
Gently suggest a more informed path, such as asking another doctor, without sounding dismissive

useful_phrases.phrase: I get why you feel that way. All the same, I'd want a second opinion.
useful_phrases.ko: 그 마음 이해해. 그래도 다른 의견은 들어보고 싶어.

useful_phrases.phrase: Honestly, the picture is a lot messier than that.
Can you live with yourself if you don't try?
True, it might work. But that doesn't mean we should skip the evidence.
useful_phrases.ko: 효과가 있을 수도 있지. 하지만 근거를 건너뛰어도 된다는 뜻은 아니야.

useful_phrases.phrase: That feels less like a plan and more like a reflex.

shadowing.reason_ko: 'do I believe this will work?'에서 'can I live with myself if I don't try?'로 대비시키는 수사 구조와 감정이 담긴 억양을 연습하기 좋다.
'less like X and more like Y'로 프레임을 바꾸고 마지막에 짧은 문장으로 핵심을 던지는 호흡이 패널 발언에 유용하다.
'True, ... But that doesn't mean...'로 양보 후 반박하는 흐름과 반대 의견 제시 방식을 연습할 수 있다.

difficulty.note_ko: 서사 위주라 속도는 적당하지만 의학, 역사, 문어체 어휘(exhume, apotropaic, posthumous 등)가 많다. 후반부 분석 구간은 논증 표현이 풍부해 말하기에 바로 쓸 수 있다.

translations_sent.0-0: 푸시킨. 코네티컷주 그리스월드라는 마을에서 아이들이 오래된 자갈 광산에서 놀고 있습니다.
translations_sent.2-2: 수년간 이어진 채굴로 이곳은 가파르고 잿빛인 비탈이 줄줄이 이어진 모습이 되었습니다.
translations_sent.3-3: 지금은 버려진 채, 동네 아이들의 썰매장이 되었죠.
translations_sent.4-4: 아이들은 장화가 자갈 위에서 미끄러지는 가운데 비탈을 기어올랐다가, 깔깔대며 비명을 지르고는 채석장 바닥으로 쏜살같이 내려옵니다.
translations_sent.5-5: 작은 돌멩이들이 아이들을 따라 후드득 굴러 내려옵니다.
translations_sent.6-6: 그러다 한 번은, 땅이 평범한 조약돌보다 훨씬 큰 무언가를 토해냅니다. 매끈하고 갈색인 무언가를요.
translations_sent.7-7: 그것은 공중에서 구르더니 바닥에 와서 멈춥니다.
translations_sent.8-8: 아이들이 호기심 어린 얼굴로 그 물체 주위에 둥글게 모여듭니다.
translations_sent.9-9: 그것은 아무것도 보지 못하는 눈으로 아이들을 올려다봅니다.
translations_sent.12-12: 흙이 빽빽이 들어찬 채 벌어진 턱.
translations_sent.15-15: 곧 노란색 범죄 현장 테이프가 이 놀이터를 둘러쌉니다.
translations_sent.16-16: 1980년대에 연쇄살인범 한 명이 코네티컷을 공포에 떨게 했습니다. 적어도 여덟 명의 여성과 소녀가 목숨을 잃었죠.
translations_sent.17-17: 경찰은 아이들이 그가 남긴 또 다른 희생자를 발견한 게 아닐까 생각합니다.
translations_sent.18-18: 하지만 이 두개골이 다른 세기의 것이라는 사실이 금세 분명해집니다.
translations_sent.19-19: 주 고고학자인 닉 벨란토니가 불려 오고, 수사는 범죄 현장에서 역사 발굴로 바뀝니다.
translations_sent.20-20: 벨란토니와 팀원들은 먼저 날이 평평한 삽으로, 그다음에는 섬세한 붓과 대나무 꼬챙이로 흙을 조금씩 걷어내기 시작하고, 언덕 비탈에서 관이 하나둘 계속 모습을 드러냅니다.
translations_sent.21-21: 관 속 유골 중 일부에는 폭력적인 부상의 흔적이 있습니다.
translations_sent.22-22: 또 어떤 유골은 두개골에 머리카락 뭉치가 아직 붙어 있습니다.
translations_sent.23-23: 한쪽 구석에는 훨씬 작은 유골 일곱 구가 한데 모여 누워 있습니다.
translations_sent.24-24: 아이들입니다. 이곳은 단순한 자갈 구덩이가 아니었던 겁니다.
translations_sent.26-26: 무덤 하나가 유독 눈에 띕니다. 광산 벽면에 석조 지하 묘실이 삐죽 튀어나와 있었거든요.
translations_sent.28-28: 그는 묘실 지붕을 이루는 납작하고 무거운 돌들을 들어내기 시작하고, 어둠 속을 들여다봅니다.
translations_sent.29-29: 안에는 붉게 칠한 나무 관이 있습니다.
translations_sent.30-30: 뚜껑은 안쪽으로 부서져 있고, 해골이 된 두 발이 드러나 있습니다.
translations_sent.31-31: 남자입니다. 앨런 토니가 돌을 하나 더 들어내고는 얼어붙습니다.
translations_sent.32-32: 이 시신에는 누군가 손을 댄 흔적이 있었습니다. 도굴꾼이나 우발적인 훼손범의 짓이 아니라, 섬뜩할 만큼 끈기 있고 음산하면서도 단 하나의 목적을 가진 누군가의 소행이었죠.
translations_sent.33-33: 남자의 흉곽은 비틀어 열려 있었고, 두개골은 척추에서 잘려 나갔으며, 넓적다리뼈는 관절에서 뽑혀 있었습니다.
translations_sent.34-34: 그 뼈들은 망가진 갈비뼈 위에 조심스럽게, 의도적으로 놓여 있었습니다.
translations_sent.35-35: 관 속을 내려다보던 벨란토니는 자신이 더 이상 평범한 무덤을 보고 있는 게 아님을 깨닫습니다. 사람의 유해로 조잡하게 만든 해골과 교차한 뼈 문양이었던 거죠.
translations_sent.36-36: 그는 이런 건 한 번도 본 적이 없습니다.
translations_sent.37-37: 저는 팀 하포드입니다. 지금 들으시는 팟캐스트는 «Cautionary Tales»입니다.
translations_sent.38-38: «Cautionary Tales» 1883년, 그리스월드에서 20마일 떨어진 곳에서는 또 다른 공동체가 나름의 수수께끼에 직면하고 있었습니다.
translations_sent.39-39: 그 일은 메리 일라이자 브라운이라는 여성에게서 시작되었습니다.
translations_sent.40-40: 그녀는 남편 조지, 그리고 일곱 아이들과 함께 로드아일랜드주 엑서터라는 작은 농촌 마을의 변두리에 살았습니다.
translations_sent.41-41: 브라운 가족은 30~40에이커쯤 되는 작은 농장을 꾸리는 부지런한 가족이었어요.
translations_sent.42-42: 이들의 삶은 계절을 따라 흘러갔습니다. 봄에는 씨를 뿌리고, 여름에는 김을 매고, 가을에는 수확을 했죠.
translations_sent.43-43: 땅이 얼어붙는 겨울에는 목재를 실어 나르고, 가축에게 먹이와 물을 주면서 해빙기를 기다렸습니다.
translations_sent.44-44: 엑서터의 토양은 얇았고, 땅은 돌투성이에 고집스러웠어요.
translations_sent.45-45: 세기 초에는 이곳에 2,500명이 살았지만, 메리 엘리자가 아이들을 키우던 무렵에는 1,000명도 채 남지 않았습니다.
translations_sent.46-46: 많은 사람들이 더 좋은 땅을 찾아 서부로 떠났고, 이제는 소나무와 참나무가 버려진 농장을 빽빽이 뒤덮으며 사람들이 두고 간 땅을 되찾고 있었죠.
translations_sent.47-47: 남은 사람들은 그 땅에서 양배추와 호박을 힘겹게 일궈 냈고, 돌담을 두른 거친 목초지에서 가축을 풀어 먹였습니다.
translations_sent.48-48: 엑서터는 살기 쉬운 곳은 아니었지만, 정겨운 곳이었어요.
translations_sent.49-49: 이웃들은 잡화점이나 술집에서 만났고, 지역 신문에는 결혼과 부고뿐 아니라 일상적인 소소한 일들도 실렸습니다.
translations_sent.50-50: 농사 중에 일어난 사고, 마을을 찾아온 손님, 그리고 누가 아파서 앓아누웠는지 같은 것들이요.
translations_sent.51-51: 하얀 판자 외벽의 교회에서는 여자들이 저녁 식사 모임과 자선 모임을 열었습니다.
translations_sent.52-52: 모두가 서로의 사정을 알았어요. 모든 사람의 일이 곧 모두에게 중요한 일이었으니까요.
translations_sent.53-53: 그래서 한 가정에 어려움이 닥치면, 그건 그 가족만의 일이 아니었습니다.
translations_sent.54-54: 1880년대 초, 메리 엘리자에게 변화가 생기기 시작했습니다.
translations_sent.55-55: 빨래나 요리 같은 평범한 집안일만 해도 그녀는 녹초가 되었어요.
translations_sent.56-56: 곧 옷이 헐렁하게 몸에 걸릴 만큼 야위었고, 오후마다 열이 올랐습니다.
translations_sent.57-57: 브라운 가족은 누군가 병이 났을 때 가족들이 으레 하는 일을 했습니다.
translations_sent.59-59: 양장점 일을 하던 큰딸 올리브는 어머니를 지극정성으로 돌봤습니다.
translations_sent.60-60: 엑서터의 의사들은 이런 병을 전에도 본 적이 있었어요.
translations_sent.61-61: 흔한 처방은 영양가 있는 음식, 대구 간유, 신선한 공기, 그리고 휴식으로 몸을 보하려는 것이었습니다.
translations_sent.62-62: 또 어떤 사람들은 진정 시럽이나 약초 추출물 같은 특허 의약품을 믿었죠.
translations_sent.63-63: 브라운 가족이 정확히 무엇을 시도했는지는 알 수 없지만, 메리 엘리자가 점점 쇠약해지는 걸 막지는 못했습니다.
translations_sent.65-65: 처음에는 그리 놀라운 일이 아니었을 겁니다.
translations_sent.66-66: 양장 일에 집안일도 있는 데다 어머니까지 간호하고 있었으니까요.
translations_sent.67-67: 하지만 곧 가족들은 다른 변화도 알아차렸습니다.
translations_sent.70-70: 밤이면 가슴을 짓누르는 숨 막힐 듯한 묵직한 압박감이라는 이상한 느낌을 호소했습니다.
translations_sent.71-71: 그 와중에도 메리 엘리자는 계속 쇠약해지고 있었어요.
translations_sent.72-72: 1883년 크리스마스 직전, 그녀는 세상을 떠났고 가족은 하얀 판자 교회 옆 묘지에 그녀를 묻었습니다.
translations_sent.73-73: 하지만 메리 엘리자를 앗아간 그것은 그녀와 함께 떠나지 않았습니다.
translations_sent.74-74: 올리브에게 기침이 생겼습니다. 처음에는 메마르고 끈질기게 몸을 쥐어짜는 기침이었지만, 곧 손수건에 핏자국이 묻어나기 시작했죠. 붉은 점 몇 개로 시작해 나중엔 찻숟가락으로 몇 번 떠낼 만큼 나왔습니다.
translations_sent.75-75: 이런 소모성 질환에는 이름이 있었습니다. 환자를 다 삼켜 버리는 것처럼 보였기 때문이죠.
translations_sent.78-78: 사람들은 이 병이 가족을 따라 번질 수 있다는 건 알았지만, 원인은 그다지 확실하지 않았습니다.
translations_sent.81-81: 또 어떤 사람들은 더 오래되고 더 기이한 생각에 매달렸죠.
translations_sent.82-82: 눈에 보이지 않는 무언가가 이 가족을 갉아먹으며 희생자에서 희생자로 옮겨 다니는 게 아닐까 하고요.
translations_sent.83-83: 조지 브라운은 그런 믿음은 전혀 상대하지 않았어요.
translations_sent.84-84: 하지만 그렇다고 딸에게 벌어지는 일이 덜 무서워지는 건 아니었죠.
translations_sent.85-85: 어머니가 세상을 떠난 지 여섯 달 뒤, 올리브는 자신의 몸이 무너져 가고 있다는 걸 알았어요.
translations_sent.86-86: 극심한 고통 속에서 숨쉬기도 힘겨워하면서, 올리브는 자신의 장례식에서 부를 찬송가를 골랐어요.
translations_sent.87-87: 1884년 6월 올리브가 스무 살의 나이로 숨졌을 때, 온 마을 사람들이 교회에 모였어요.
translations_sent.88-88: 사람들은 함께 일어나 감미롭고도 엄숙한 생각을 담은 노래를 불렀죠.
translations_sent.89-89: 그 뒤 몇 년 동안 브라운 가족은 익숙한 일상에 의지하며 지냈어요.
translations_sent.90-90: 계절은 늘 그랬듯 흘러갔고, 가을엔 수확을, 봄엔 파종을 했죠.
translations_sent.91-91: 조지 브라운은 소 거래를 했고, 농장은 점점 커졌어요.
translations_sent.92-92: 딸 머시 레나, 흔히 레나라고 불리던 그녀는 바느질하고, 옷을 깁고, 있는 것으로 꾸려 나가는 집안일을 배웠어요.
translations_sent.93-93: 레나는 동생인 해티, 제니와 함께 동네 주일학교에서 노래도 불렀어요.
translations_sent.94-94: 아들 에디 브라운은 키 크고 튼튼한 청년으로 자랐어요.
translations_sent.95-95: 에디는 동네 악단에 들어갔는데, 이 악단의 행진곡과 폴카는 엑서터 사교 생활의 배경음악이었고, 장터와 야외 파티에서 인기가 많았죠.
translations_sent.96-96: 에디는 들에서 아버지를 도왔고, 잡화점에서 점원 일도 구했으며, 마을에서 사람들에게 호감을 샀어요.
translations_sent.98-98: 그는 동네 교회에서 결혼해서, 신부 호르텐스와 함께 마을 외곽의 새집으로 이사했어요.
translations_sent.99-99: 결혼식 직후, 그의 악단이 찾아와 집을 음악으로 가득 채웠죠.
translations_sent.104-104: 19세기 뉴잉글랜드에서 폐결핵은 사망 원인 1위였고, 네 명 중 한 명의 목숨을 앗아갔어요.
translations_sent.105-105: 엑서터 사람들에게 그 병은 무섭고 수수께끼 같은 존재였죠.
translations_sent.106-106: 하지만 사람들이 나쁜 공기냐 나쁜 혈통이냐를 두고 논쟁하는 동안, 과학은 진짜 범인에게 다가가고 있었어요.
translations_sent.107-107: 1860년대에 프랑스 의사 장앙투안 빌맹은 소모병이라고도 불리는 폐결핵이 침입한 병원체가 일으키는 전염병이라는 걸 증명했어요.
translations_sent.108-108: 그리고 1882년, 메리 일라이자가 세상을 떠나기 전해에, 로베르트 코흐라는 독일 의사가 현미경을 들여다보다가 유리 커버슬립 위에 푸르게 염색된 가느다란 막대 모양을 발견했어요.
translations_sent.109-109: 바로 결핵균, 그 병을 일으키는 생물체였죠.
translations_sent.110-110: 괴물이 브라운 가족을 갉아먹고 있었던 거예요.
translations_sent.111-111: 보이지 않는 건 아니었지만 아주아주 작았고, 이제는 연구할 수 있게 되었죠.
translations_sent.112-112: 코흐의 발견은 세균설의 커다란 승리였지만, 그의 연구 결과는 아직 새로운 것이었어요. 뉴잉글랜드까지는 전해졌어도 모든 마을에, 하물며 모든 농가에까지 스며들지는 못했죠.
translations_sent.113-113: 그래도 에디 브라운이 병에 걸릴 무렵에는 의사들이 무엇을 상대하는지 더 잘 알게 되었어요.
translations_sent.114-114: 창문 열기, 휴식, 따뜻한 기후는 오래전부터 폐결핵 처방으로 쓰였어요.
translations_sent.115-115: 이제 이런 처방에 새로운 과학적 논리가 더해졌죠.
translations_sent.116-116: 전염성 있는 무언가가 사람들 사이에 옮겨 다니는 거라면, 신선하고 움직이는 공기가 그것을 막아 주는 데 도움이 될 수 있다는 거였어요.
translations_sent.117-117: 의사들은 환자들에게 공기가 맑고 기후가 화창하고 건조한 산으로 가라고 권했어요.
translations_sent.118-118: 안내 책자들은 아픈 사람들을 '새로운 폐의 땅'으로 초대하며, 서부로 와서 살라고 간청했죠.
translations_sent.119-119: 캘리포니아와 콜로라도의 도시들은 이른바 '렁거'라고 불리는 폐병 환자들로 가득 찼어요.
translations_sent.120-120: 애디론댁과 다른 산악 휴양지들에는 전문 요양소들이 문을 열었어요.
translations_sent.121-121: 이곳에서 환자들은 가능한 한 많은 시간을 야외에서 맑은 공기를 쐬며 쉬면서 보냈죠.
translations_sent.124-124: 조지 브라운은 결핵을 이미 두 번이나 겪은 적이 있었어요.
translations_sent.126-126: 두 사람 모두 그의 손으로 묻었어요.
translations_sent.127-127: 그런데 이제는 아들이 병에 걸린 거예요.
translations_sent.128-128: 에디는 스물두 살에 결혼도 했고, 스스로 자기 길을 개척해 가던 중이었어요.
translations_sent.129-129: 산으로 떠난다는 건 사랑하는 가족과 일, 그리고 가족 농장을 떠난다는 뜻이었죠.
translations_sent.130-130: 하지만 결국 브라운 가족은 그럴 만한 가치가 있다고 결정했어요.
translations_sent.132-132: 에디는 아마 기차를 타고 갔을 거예요. 뉴잉글랜드의 푸른 언덕이 광활하고 평평한 대초원으로 바뀌다가, 마침내 지평선 위로 로키산맥이 솟아오르는 걸 바라보았겠죠.
translations_sent.133-133: 그가 도착한 곳은 손길이 닿지 않은 황무지가 아니라, 모두 건강해지려는 같은 이유로 몰려든 사람들로 북적이는 신생 도시였어요.
translations_sent.134-134: 많은 사람들이 결핵 환자가 잠을 잘 수 있도록 특별한 베란다가 딸린 하숙집에 머물렀어요.
translations_sent.135-135: 또 어떤 사람들은 야외의 천막에서 지냈죠.
translations_sent.137-137: 몇 달 뒤에는 아내 호텐스가 그를 따라왔는데, 믿음직한 그의 옛 고용주가 동행해 줬어요.
translations_sent.138-138: 호텐스의 보살핌과 콜로라도의 기후가 함께 마법을 부리는 듯했어요.
translations_sent.139-139: 에디의 뺨에 혈색이 돌아왔고, 앙상했던 몸도 차츰 살이 올랐어요.
translations_sent.140-140: 기침은 계속됐지만, 시내 전차 차장으로 일할 수 있을 만큼은 건강해졌죠.
translations_sent.141-141: 에디가 기쁘게도 호전되고 있다는 소식이 엑서터에도 전해졌어요.
translations_sent.144-144: 에디의 여동생 리나가 빠르게 쇠약해지고 있었거든요.
translations_sent.145-145: 리나의 건강 문제는 1890년 여름, 에디가 집을 떠나기 직전에 시작됐어요.
translations_sent.146-146: 왜 리나가 오빠와 함께 콜로라도에 가지 않았는지는 확실하지 않아요.
translations_sent.147-147: 브라운 가족 중 한 명이 먼 길을 떠날 돈밖에 없었을 수도 있고, 너무 약해서 여행하기 어렵다고 판단됐을 수도 있어요.
translations_sent.148-148: 어쨌든 리나는 엑서터에 남았고, 1891년 11월이 되자 지역 질병 기록에는 그녀의 상태가 매우 위중하다고 적혀 있었어요.
translations_sent.149-149: 조지 브라운은 그 지역 최고의 의사 중 한 명으로 널리 알려진 해럴드 메트캐프 박사를 불렀어요.
translations_sent.150-150: 그는 몇 년간 뉴욕시 벨뷰 병원에서 일하면서, 매일 거리를 질주하던 말이 끄는 구급마차에 올라 환자들을 돌봤던 사람이었어요.
translations_sent.151-151: 경험이 많고 현실적인 의사였지만, 그는 리나를 진찰한 뒤 아버지 조지에게 그녀를 살리기 위해 할 수 있는 일이 없다고 말했어요.
translations_sent.153-153: 의사들은 기침을 가라앉히고 통증을 덜어 주려고 모르핀과 아편을 썼어요.
translations_sent.154-154: 하지만 이 단계가 되자 리나의 폐는 심하게 손상되어 있었어요.
translations_sent.156-156: 혹독하게 추운 한겨울의 어느 날, 조지 브라운은 두 번째 딸을 아내 곁에 묻었어요.
translations_sent.158-158: 리나는 교회 묘지의 납골실에 안치되었고, 봄에 땅이 녹을 때까지 거기에 있게 됐어요.
translations_sent.159-159: 리나가 묻히고 한 달 뒤, 에디와 호텐스가 엑서터로 돌아왔어요. 에디가 완전히 건강을 되찾아서가 아니라, 상태가 더 나빠졌기 때문이었죠.
translations_sent.160-160: 콜로라도의 기후도 더 이상 그를 낫게 해 주지 못하는 것 같았습니다.
translations_sent.161-161: 그는 먼 길을 어떻게든 버텨 냈지만, 로드아일랜드에 도착했을 때는 녹초가 되어 있었습니다.
translations_sent.162-162: 에디는 고향에서 정말로 사랑받는 사람이었고, 지역 신문에도 그런 애정이 고스란히 드러났습니다.
translations_sent.163-163: 수많은 친구들의 좋은 바람과 기도가 이루어진다면, 우리의 친구 에디는 곧 완전히 건강을 되찾을 것이라고 했죠.
translations_sent.164-164: 에디의 이웃 몇몇은 그 기도를 현실로 만들 방법을 안다고 생각했습니다.
translations_sent.165-165: 조지 브라운이 아직 시도해 보지 않은 오래된 초자연적 치료법이 있었고, 이웃들은 그것이 그의 아들을 살릴 수도 있다고 믿었습니다.
translations_sent.166-166: 그 지역의 관습에서는 한 가족에게 폐병이 휩쓸고 지나가면 그건 단순한 병이 아니라, 죽은 자들이 무덤 너머에서 손을 뻗어 산 사람의 기운을 빨아먹는 것이라고 여겼습니다.
translations_sent.167-167: 에디에게 일어나는 일이 바로 그것이라면, 그 흡혈을 멈출 방법은 단 하나뿐이었습니다.
translations_sent.168-168: 교회 묘지로 가서 메리 일라이자, 올리브, 리나의 무덤을 열고 그 원인을 없애 버리는 것이었죠.
translations_sent.169-169: 이웃들은 조지를 찾아가 필요한 조치를 취해도 되겠느냐고 허락을 구했습니다.
translations_sent.170-170: 조지는 그들의 절박함을 이해했을 겁니다. 하지만 그렇게 끔찍한 부탁을 들어줄 수는 없었습니다.
translations_sent.172-172: 1년간의 발굴 끝에 닉 벨란토니와 그의 팀은 29명의 유해를 찾아냈습니다.
translations_sent.173-173: 그곳은 작은 농장 묘지였고, 여러 세대의 가족들이 나란히 묻혀 있었습니다. 납골 구덩이에서 나온 유골, 그러니까 두개골과 대퇴골이 교차하는 모양으로 공들여 배열된 그 유골은 JB라고 불리게 되었는데, 관 뚜껑에 황동 징으로 JB55라는 글자가 새겨져 있었기 때문입니다. 벨란토니는 JB를 국립 보건의학 박물관으로 보냈습니다.
translations_sent.174-174: 워싱턴 DC에서 이루어진 조사 결과, 그는 19세기 초에 55세쯤에 사망한 것으로 밝혀졌습니다.
translations_sent.175-175: 그는 관절염을 앓았고, 다른 병도 있었습니다.
translations_sent.176-176: 갈비뼈 곳곳에 창백하고 움푹 팬 병변이 있었는데, 이는 흉통과 기침을 일으켰을 만성 폐 감염의 흔적이었습니다.
translations_sent.177-177: JB는 거의 확실하게 결핵으로 사망했던 겁니다.
translations_sent.178-178: 게다가 법의학 검사 결과, JB의 뼈를 다시 배열했을 때 뼈에는 살이 하나도 남아 있지 않았습니다.
translations_sent.179-179: 시신은 이미 완전히 분해된 상태였던 거죠.
translations_sent.180-180: 두개골과 대퇴골을 교차시킨 그 의식이 무엇이었든, 그가 죽은 직후에 행해진 건 아니었습니다.
translations_sent.181-181: 적어도 5년 이상 지난 뒤에 이루어진 것이었죠.
translations_sent.182-182: 벨란토니는 이것이 일종의 의식이라는 걸 알았고, 그 의미를 풀기 위해 민속학자 마이클 벨에게 도움을 청했습니다.
translations_sent.183-183: 벨은 18~19세기 뉴잉글랜드 전역에서 일어난 묘지 훼손 사건을 수년간 연구해 왔고, 벨란토니에게 뚜렷한 패턴이 있다고 말했습니다.
translations_sent.184-184: 폐병이 한 가족을 쓰러뜨리면, 사람들이 때로는 죽은 이들을 찾아가 무덤을 열었다는 겁니다.
translations_sent.187-187: 1892년 엑서터, 에디 브라운은 점점 더 쇠약해졌습니다.
translations_sent.188-188: 그와 가족 모두 병이 마지막 작업을 하고 있다는 걸 알고 있었습니다.
translations_sent.189-189: 아침이면 그는 식은땀에 흠뻑 젖은 채 눈을 떴습니다.
translations_sent.190-190: 기침할 때마다 가슴이 찢어지는 듯했고, 폐가 피와 고름으로 차오르면서 숨을 쉬는 단순한 일조차 힘겨운 싸움이었습니다.
translations_sent.191-191: 엑서터 사람들은 다시 조지를 찾아와 같은 부탁을 되풀이했습니다.
translations_sent.192-192: 이번에는 조지가 아들 에디와 이야기를 나눴습니다.
translations_sent.194-194: 남자들이 삽을 들고 메리 일라이자, 올리브, 리나의 무덤 앞에 모였습니다.
translations_sent.197-197: 해럴드 메트캘프 박사는 문을 열었다가 잔뜩 흥분한 한 청년을 맞닥뜨렸습니다.
translations_sent.198-198: 청년은 에디 브라운이 죽어 가고 있으며, 그를 살리려고 엑서터 마을 사람 몇 명이 메리 일라이자 브라운의 시신을 파냈다고 말했습니다.
translations_sent.199-199: 청년은 메트캘프가 와서 그녀의 유해를 살펴봐 주기를 원했습니다.
translations_sent.200-200: 그러고는 다른 말을 중얼거렸어요. 피에 대해서, 그리고 죽은 가족이 돌아와 산 사람들을 먹이로 삼는다는 이야기였죠.
translations_sent.202-202: 그는 과학을 하는 사람이었고, 에디 브라운을 치료한 적은 없었지만 에디의 누이 리나가 폐결핵으로 죽었다는 건 알고 있었어요.
translations_sent.203-203: 브라운 집안 무덤 어디에도 불가사의할 건 없었습니다.
translations_sent.205-205: 얼마 지나지 않아 그 청년이 다시 돌아왔는데, 이번에는 조지 브라운의 전갈을 가지고 왔습니다.
translations_sent.206-206: 그 농부는 자신은 어떤 미신도 믿지 않는다고 분명히 말했지만, 그래도 메트칼프가 죽은 아내와 딸들의 시신을 해부해 주기를 바랐어요.
translations_sent.209-209: 교회 묘지에는 남자들이 열린 무덤 옆에서 기다리고 있었습니다.
translations_sent.210-210: 메트칼프는 메리 일라이자가 이미 파헤쳐져 있는 걸 보았어요.
translations_sent.211-211: 그녀의 시신은 몇 년 동안 땅속에 있으면서 말라붙고 쪼그라들어 있었습니다.
translations_sent.213-213: 하지만 거기 있던 사람들 가운데에는 프로비던스 저널의 기자가 한 명 있었습니다.
translations_sent.214-214: 훗날 그는 메리 일라이자의 시신이 미라처럼 변해 있었다고 묘사했죠.
translations_sent.215-215: 남자들은 죽은 사람과 산 사람을 잇는 고리라고 여겨지던 액체 상태의 피를 찾아보라고 메트칼프를 불렀던 겁니다.
translations_sent.216-216: 그는 사람들이 두 번째 무덤, 올리브의 무덤에 삽을 대는 걸 지켜보았어요.
translations_sent.217-217: 하지만 관 뚜껑을 비틀어 열었을 때는 살펴볼 게 아무것도 없었습니다. 마른 뼈와 남아 있는 머리카락 한 뭉치뿐이었죠.
translations_sent.219-219: 어머니나 언니와 달리 리나는 땅에 묻히지 않았습니다.
translations_sent.220-220: 대신 겨울이 지나기를 기다리며 차가운 돌 납골당에 안치되어 있었어요.
translations_sent.221-221: 남자들이 납골당을 열었고, 눈앞의 광경에 깜짝 놀랐습니다.
translations_sent.222-222: 죽은 지 두 달이 지났는데도 리나는 놀랄 만큼 거의 변하지 않았어요.
translations_sent.225-225: 그는 메스를 들고 앞으로 나가 리나의 몸통을 조심스럽게 절개하고 심장을 꺼냈습니다.
translations_sent.229-229: 액체 상태의 피였어요. 메트칼프는 여기에 초자연적인 건 전혀 없다는 걸 알았고, 리나의 몸이 부패하지 않은 건 정상이라고 설명하려 했습니다.
translations_sent.230-230: 그녀는 죽은 지 두 달밖에 안 됐고, 차가운 곳에 보관되어 있었으니까요.
translations_sent.231-231: 그는 흉터 조직으로 가득한 폐도 가리켜 보였어요.
translations_sent.232-232: 하지만 마을 사람들은 찾던 것을 찾아낸 거였죠. 폐병으로 죽은 여자의 심장 속 피를요.
translations_sent.233-233: 그들에게 이건 리나 브라운의 일부가 죽지 않은 채 남아 오빠의 생명을 빨아먹고 있다는 증거였습니다.
translations_sent.235-235: 메리와 일라이자, 올리브는 리나가 병에 걸리기 훨씬 전에 죽었다는 거죠.
translations_sent.236-236: 리나가 그들을 먹이로 삼았을 리가 없었습니다.
translations_sent.237-237: 하지만 에디가 아직 살아 있으면서 점점 쇠약해지고 있고, 이제 그걸 막기 위해 할 수 있는 일이 생겼다는 사실에 비하면 그건 별로 중요하지 않았는지도 모릅니다.
translations_sent.238-238: 오래된 믿음에 따르면, 죽은 사람의 심장에 피가 남아 있는 한 가족들은 계속 죽어 간다고 했어요.
translations_sent.239-239: 그래서... 바로 그 교회 묘지에서 남자들은 불을 피우고 리나의 심장을 불길 속에 던져 재가 될 때까지 타는 걸 지켜보았습니다.
translations_sent.240-240: 의식에 따르면, 에디 브라운은 그 재를 강장제에 타서 마셔야 했어요.
translations_sent.242-242: 2019년, 닉 벨란토니가 JB를 발굴한 지 거의 30년이 지나서야 연구진은 마침내 그가 누구였을지 범위를 좁힐 수 있었어요.
translations_sent.243-243: DNA 프로파일링과 족보 기록을 이용해, 그가 1800년대에 그 지역에 살았던 존 바버라는 농부였을 가능성이 높다고 결론지었죠.
translations_sent.244-244: JB 가까이에서 연구팀은 NB13이라고 표시된 더 작은 관을 하나 더 발견했어요. 거의 확실히 바버의 아들 네이선이었고, 십대 초반에 세상을 떠난 아이였죠.
translations_sent.245-245: 벨란토니는 두개골과 대퇴골을 X자로 놓는 의식이 악을 물리치기 위한 일종의 마법, 즉 액막이 처방이었을 거라는 이론을 세웠어요.
translations_sent.247-247: 대서양 건너편에서는 시신이 부풀어 있고, 머리카락과 손톱이 계속 자라는 것처럼 보이며, 심장과 흉강에 피가 남아 있는 채로 발견되는 경우가 가끔 있었어요.
translations_sent.248-248: 이런 현상은 모두 자연적인 설명이 가능했지만, 부패 과정을 이해하지 못하는 사람들에게는 죽은 자가 아직 산 자와의 관계를 끝내지 않았다는 신호처럼 보일 수 있었죠.
translations_sent.249-249: 누군가 존 바버를 찾아왔을 때는 살펴볼 심장이 이미 남아 있지 않았어요.
translations_sent.251-251: 그래서 그의 무덤을 다시 찾은 사람은 죽은 자가 돌아오지 못하게 하는 또 다른 오래된 관습을 택했어요.
translations_sent.252-252: 그의 두개골과 다리뼈를 몸에서 떼어 놓은 거예요.
translations_sent.253-253: 몇 년 뒤인 1892년, 리나 브라운이 같은 절박한 희망의 대상이 되었어요.
translations_sent.254-254: 이 이야기는 묘하게 사람을 사로잡아서, 대서양을 건너가기까지 했어요.
translations_sent.255-255: 1912년, 리나의 시신 발굴을 자세히 다룬 신문 기사 조각이 『드라큘라』의 작가 브램 스토커의 사후 개인 문서들 사이에 끼워진 채 발견됐어요.
translations_sent.256-256: 《프로비던스 저널》은 이 발굴 의식을 비웃는 투로 다루면서 선정적인 뱀파이어 소동으로 부풀렸어요.
translations_sent.257-257: 엑서터 사람들 중 누군가 실제로 뱀파이어라는 말을 썼거나, 자신들이 그런 것을 상대한다고 믿었는지는 분명하지 않아요.
translations_sent.258-258: 그런데도 그 신문은 고딕풍의 상투적 표현을 써서, 과학보다 미신을 택한 무지한 시골뜨기라고 마을 사람들을 조롱했죠.
translations_sent.259-259: 제 생각에 실제 모습은 훨씬 더 복잡하고 훨씬 더 인간적이에요.
translations_sent.260-260: 맞아요, 리나의 무덤을 연 사람들은 의사들만큼 결핵을 이해하지 못했어요.
translations_sent.262-262: 하지만 그렇다고 그들의 결정이 과학과 미신 사이의 단순한 대결이었다는 뜻은 아니에요.
translations_sent.263-263: 코흐가 결핵균을 발견한 건 하나의 사실이었죠.
translations_sent.264-264: 하지만 결핵을 진단하고, 확산을 막고, 치료하고, 결국 완치하는 법을 알아내기까지는 수십 년이 걸렸고, 과학적 발견 이상의 것이 필요했어요.
translations_sent.265-265: 공중보건 체계, 더 나은 주거, 위생 시설, 새로운 간호 방식, 교육, 그리고 일상 행동의 수백만 가지 작은 변화가 필요했죠.
translations_sent.266-266: 브라운 가족은 무엇이 사람들을 죽이는지 과학이 이해한 시점과 그것을 막는 법을 알게 된 시점 사이의 긴 공백 속에 살았어요.
translations_sent.267-267: 겉으로 보면 조지 브라운이 발굴을 허락한 결정은 모순처럼 보여요.
translations_sent.268-268: 그는 현대 의사를 찾아다니고, 아들을 서부로 보내고, 옛 민간 신앙은 믿지 않는다고 주장한 현실적인 농부였으니까요.
translations_sent.270-270: 엑서터는 작고 서로 긴밀하게 연결된 곳이었고, 아마 그게 그의 결정에 영향을 줬을 거예요.
translations_sent.271-271: 이웃들은 지역 신문에서 병상에 누운 사람들의 소식을 읽고 아픈 사람들을 지켜봐 주었어요.
translations_sent.272-272: 농사일을 도와주고, 결혼을 축하하고, 장례식에 함께 모였죠.
translations_sent.273-273: 조지는 그들의 믿음 중 일부를 이상하게 여겼을지 몰라도, 이들은 그가 아는 사람들이고, 의지하는 사람들이고, 에디가 떠난 뒤에도, 만약 떠난다면요, 함께 살아가야 할 사람들이었어요. 그런데 여기엔 다른 무언가도 작용하지 않았을까 싶어요.
translations_sent.274-274: 의료 사회학자들은 가끔 치료 강박이라고 불리는 일종의 행동 편향에 대해 이야기해요.
translations_sent.275-275: 죽어가는 환자를 계속 치료해야 한다는 압박인데, 그 개입이 큰 고통을 동반하고 성공 가능성이 거의 없을 때조차 그렇죠.
translations_sent.276-276: 의사도, 환자도, 가족도 이걸 느낄 수 있어요. 어떤 처치가 존재한다는 사실 자체가 그걸 시도해야 한다는 강한 느낌을 만들어 낼 수 있거든요.
translations_sent.277-277: 이 개념은 보통 현대 의학과 그 기술적 발전과 연결돼요.
translations_sent.278-278: 조지 브라운에게는 기계로 가득한 중환자실도, 약물이 즐비한 선택지도 없었어요.
translations_sent.279-279: 그래도 저는 치료 강박이 그가 직면한 딜레마를 이해하는 데 도움이 된다고 생각해요.
translations_sent.280-280: 조지에게 아무것도 하지 않는다는 건 단순히 행동이 없는 상태라기보다, 아들을 일부러 죽게 내버려 두기로 선택하는 것처럼 느껴졌을지도 모릅니다.
translations_sent.281-281: 그 의식은 의학이 줄 수 없던 것, 그러니까 자기가 직접 할 수 있는 일을 그에게 주었습니다.
translations_sent.282-282: 어쩌면 질문은 더 이상 '이게 효과가 있을 거라고 믿는가?'가 아니었을지도 모릅니다.
translations_sent.283-283: 대신 이렇게 바뀐 거죠. '시도조차 하지 않고서 내가 나 자신과 함께 살아갈 수 있을까?'
translations_sent.284-284: 1892년 5월, 무덤을 파헤친 지 두 달 뒤에 조지 브라운은 아들을 묻었습니다.
translations_sent.286-286: 부고에는 그가 훌륭한 인품을 지닌 청년이며 어떤 공동체도 잃기 아까운 사람이라고 적혀 있었고, 장례식에는 하얀 판자 외벽의 교회가 사람들로 가득 찼습니다.
translations_sent.287-287: 지역의 직물 공방에서는 '남편이자 동료'라는 글귀가 새겨진 쿠션을 보냈습니다.
translations_sent.288-288: 관은 꽃으로 덮였고, 그의 옛 고용주가 보낸 '사랑하는 이들과 헤어지며'라는 문구의 화환도 있었으며, 성가대는 찬송가 '언젠가 달콤한 날'을 불렀습니다.
translations_sent.289-289: 조지 브라운은 아내와 세 자녀를 잃었습니다.
translations_sent.290-290: 그는 이후에도 세 딸 애니, 제니, 마이라를 더 묻게 되고, 오직 해티만이 그보다 오래 살았습니다.
translations_sent.291-291: 그는 이후 30년을 더 엑서터에서 살았는데, 아들을 살리려고 아내와 딸들의 무덤을 열었던 바로 그 이웃들과 나란히 지냈습니다.
translations_sent.292-292: 그 시간 동안 세상은 크게 변했습니다.
translations_sent.293-293: 엑스레이는 인체 내부를 들여다보는 창을 열어 주었고, 과학자들은 최초의 결핵 백신을 개발했습니다.
translations_sent.295-295: 그런 건 아직 아무것도 존재하지 않았습니다.
translations_sent.296-296: 에디의 장례식에서 성가대는 또 다른 종류의 희망을 노래했습니다.
translations_sent.297-297: 머지않아, 어느 달콤한 날, 우리는 먼저 떠난 사랑하는 이들을 만나리라.
translations_sent.299-299: 참고 자료 전체 목록은 timharford.com의 쇼 노트에서 확인하실 수 있습니다.
translations_sent.300-300: 'Cautionary Tales'는 저 팀 하포드가 앤드루 라이트, 앨리스 파인스, 라이언 딜리와 함께 썼습니다.
translations_sent.301-301: 제작은 조지아 밀스와 매릴린 러스트가 맡았습니다.
translations_sent.302-302: 사운드 디자인과 오리지널 음악은 파스칼 와이즈의 작품입니다.
translations_sent.304-304: 제이콥 와이스버그, 그레타 코언, 코린 길리어드피셔, 에릭 샌들러, 크리스티나 설리번, 키라 포지, 오언 밀러의 작업이 없었다면 이 프로그램도 불가능했을 겁니다.
translations_sent.306-306: 이 프로그램이 마음에 드신다면 공유하고, 평점과 리뷰도 남겨 주세요.
translations_sent.308-308: 그리고 광고 없이 듣고 싶으시거나, 매달 보너스 오디오 에피소드와 영상 에피소드, 멤버 전용 뉴스레터를 받고 싶으시다면 Cautionary Club에 가입해 보시는 건 어떨까요?
